units.text: Start with why interruption happens. AWS can reclaim spare capacity, and a configured price ceiling can affect eligibility. A low price or accepted Spot request does not promise future capacity.

Look at the warning panel. Interruption notices are best effort, usually providing two minutes before a stop or termination. Hibernation begins immediately, so do not design recovery around a guaranteed two-minute window.

Move to application recovery. Use retryable work, save checkpoints to durable storage, and make repeated processing safe. Drain work when possible, but assume an interruption could arrive before cleanup finishes.

Inspect diversification. Multiple suitable instance types and Availability Zones improve the available choices. A capacity-aware strategy and Capacity Rebalancing can help, but neither guarantees replacement capacity.

With the full slide visible, separate the lifecycle actions. Canceling a Spot request and terminating a running instance are different operations. Verify both states, and judge the design by whether work recovers safely after interruption.

Compare shared tenancy and Dedicated Instances. Shared tenancy may place instances on hardware used by other customers. Dedicated Instances isolate hardware to your account, but do not provide host-level placement visibility or host affinity.

Move to Dedicated Hosts. You allocate a physical server with host visibility and placement controls. This can support eligible per-socket or per-core licenses, but the license terms still require validation.

Look at host affinity. It links an instance to a particular host for later starts. Auto-placement instead allows eligible launches onto available compatible hosts; choose the placement behavior deliberately.

With the complete slide restored, plan recovery. Supported host recovery can allocate a replacement in the same Availability Zone, and recovered instances establish affinity with that host. Check recovery eligibility, software support, license conditions and cost together.

Begin with cluster placement. Supported instances are placed close together in one Availability Zone for low latency and high throughput. A single rack is not guaranteed, and the slower instance limits the pair's throughput.

Compare rack-level spread. It separates underlying hardware for small critical fleets, with up to seven running instances per Availability Zone in a group. The group can span Zones; host-level spread is an Outposts option.

Move to partition placement. Each partition has its own racks, with up to seven partitions per Availability Zone. Use partition information to separate application replicas; the placement policy does not create those replicas for you.

With the full slide restored, follow the change sequence. Stop the instance, modify its placement, then start it. Compatible capacity must be available, so a launch or restart can fail. Placement controls locality or hardware separation, not application recovery.
